summary: The 25-year satellite fire record is broken. MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) see the same fires differently: VIIRS's 375 m pixels catch several times more hotspots than MODIS's 1 km pixels, so every fire trend jumps in 2012, just as MODIS nears the end of its mission. FireLedger fixes the record. We harmonized all 548 million NASA FIRMS hotspots (Terra, Aqua, S-NPP, NOAA-20) into one unit, NOAA-20 VIIRS-equivalent, with a calibration chain learned on the overlap years: hierarchical shrinkage from 1° cells to 5° blocks to global, matched observation days, separate factors for industrial heat, and a weight on every single hotspot. Draw any area on Earth and get its burning calendar since November 2000, this month against its normal (robust z-score), the last 30 days, fire season and critical months ahead, Theil-Sen trend, people living near frequent fires, and a CSV of every hotspot with its weight. Nothing is claimed without a test: leave-one-year-out cross-validation gives 4.0% error by region and month (77% uncorrected), conformal 90% bands cover 89%, the 2012 jump falls from +335% to -0.9% worldwide, and two independent checks agree: MODIS burned area and India's official Punjab crop-fire counts (ρ = 0.885). Live app, open API, open code.
details:
FireLedger: one harmonized fire record across two satellite eras

THE PROBLEM

For a quarter of a century, NASA's MODIS sensors on Terra and Aqua have been the backbone of global active-fire monitoring. In 2012 VIIRS arrived, first on Suomi NPP and then on NOAA-20, with 375 m pixels that resolve small, cool and short-lived fires that MODIS's 1 km footprint never registers. Naively concatenating the two archives creates a structural discontinuity: global hotspot counts jump by roughly +335% at the 2012 transition. That artefact contaminates every trend, anomaly, climatology and seasonal comparison spanning the switch, and the problem is now urgent: Suomi NPP stopped delivering fire data on 2 November 2026 and MODIS is approaching end of mission.

WHAT WE BUILT

FireLedger is a sensor-agnostic, harmonized active-fire record delivered as a web app (https://fireledger.vercel.app), a public REST API (https://dhruv-deku--fireledger-web.us-east.modal.run) and an open, reproducible pipeline (https://github.com/Dhruv-Deku/fireledger). We ingested all 548 million NASA FIRMS detections from November 2000 to 13 November 2026 (MODIS Collection 6.1 from Terra and Aqua; VIIRS 375 m from S-NPP and NOAA-20, archive plus near-real-time) and expressed every detection in a single reference unit: NOAA-20 VIIRS-equivalent hotspots.

FEATURES

- Arbitrary geometry: nine presets, or draw a box, circle or free polygon; exact point-in-polygon via ray casting accelerated by a 0.05° cell mask.

- Burning-activity calendar (month x year heatmap), switchable to a climatological anomaly view (each month vs the median of the same calendar month).

- Current month vs normal: median, interquartile range, percentage departure and a robust z-score based on the median absolute deviation (MAD); partial months are compared like-for-like on the same days.

- Last 30 days, day by day, against the same calendar days across 26 prior years.

- Busiest months and years, fire-season onset, peak and cessation, and critical periods ahead.

- Trend estimation: non-parametric Theil-Sen slope with Mann-Kendall (Kendall tau) significance, plus a VIIRS-only trend since 2012 containing no conversion at all.

- Exposure: WorldPop 2020 (1 km) population aggregated to 0.25° cells and stratified by fire recurrence.

- MODIS-only detections: hotspots with no VIIRS counterpart within max(1 km, along-scan pixel size) on the same UTC day (haversine distance).

- Quality flags: blind-spot months (VIIRS/MODIS ratio >= 8), MODIS orbital-drift years, provisional near-real-time data, industrial share.

- Exports: per-hotspot CSV with each detection's harmonization weight and 90% interval, monthly CSV, calendar PNG.

METHOD

- Calibration chain MODIS (Terra/Aqua) -> Suomi NPP -> NOAA-20; each link estimated only on the sensors' overlap years and only on days both instruments actually observed the cell (matched sampling), so differences in revisit, swath geometry and cloud gaps do not leak into the factors.

- Conversion factors resolved per 1° cell x calendar month x day/night overpass, regularized by hierarchical, empirical-Bayes-style shrinkage toward the 5° block and then the global estimate wherever local evidence is sparse.

- Per-hotspot weights rather than gridded scaling: any polygon and any date range reduces to an exact sum of weights, with no edge or resampling artefacts.

- Persistent industrial heat sources (recurrent-detection cell mask with a 3x3 buffer plus FIRMS static-source types 1-3 at 0.05°) receive separate factors fitted under a mass-balance constraint, and can be filtered out.

- Uncertainty quantification: split-conformal 90% prediction intervals, calibrated per spatial scale and latitude band.

- Model selection: a vectorized re-implementation of the fitting scored 166,404 hyper-parameter combinations; quantile mapping, an FRP-aware (fire radiative power) adjustment and month pooling were evaluated in an ablation study and rejected because they added little or biased key burning seasons.

VALIDATION

- Leave-one-year-out cross-validation over 2012-2019: 4.0% weighted absolute percentage error (WAPE) per region-month, versus 77% for uncorrected MODIS; 89% empirical coverage of the nominal 90% conformal bands.

- Structural-break analysis: the 2012 step collapses from +335% (raw merge) to -0.9% worldwide; a Pettitt change-point test no longer detects a break at the sensor transition; 17 of 20 GFED world regions fall within 5%.

- Independent corroboration: hotspot density per km² of MODIS burned area (MCD64) stays continuous across 2012, and its Spearman correlation with burned area rises from -0.46 (raw) to +0.78 (harmonized); India's official Punjab crop-residue fire counts (CREAMS) track our daily series with Spearman rho = 0.885.

- Year-block bootstrap (1,000 resamples) yields each area's residual 2012 uncertainty, surfaced as a reliability badge (good / fair / caution).

- Honest limits: where burning lies largely below MODIS's detection threshold (Northern Europe, boreal Canada), fires that were never observed cannot be back-cast; the app states this instead of hiding it.

IMPACT

FireLedger gives emergency responders, fire managers, land managers and climate scientists one continuous, quantitatively validated fire history, so this month can be compared fairly with any month since 2000, regardless of which satellite was in orbit, and the record survives the MODIS end of mission.

CREATIVITY AND DESIGN CHOICES

Instead of one global scaling factor, we treat harmonization as a statistical calibration problem with spatial, seasonal and diurnal structure, attach the correction to every individual detection, and expose uncertainty and reliability alongside every number.

TOOLS

Python, DuckDB over cell-sorted Parquet (548M rows), FastAPI with response caching, Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, MapLibre GL, ECharts, Tailwind CSS; serverless hosting on Modal and Vercel.

USE OF SI

We used AI coding assistants (large language models) to help write and review code, documentation and this text. The team chose the method, ran the pipeline and verified every result against the data.

SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE

- Ingestion: FIRMS archive and near-real-time CSVs for MODIS C6.1 (Terra, Aqua) and VIIRS 375 m (S-NPP, NOAA-20) are normalized into one schema (sensor, satellite, UTC timestamp, day/night flag, confidence, FRP, scan/track pixel size, static-source type).

- Storage: 548 million detections in columnar Parquet, sorted by grid cell so that spatial queries prune row groups; queried in-process with DuckDB, giving interactive aggregation without a database server.

- Harmonization layer: factor tables (cell x month x day/night, with 5° and global fallbacks) are joined to each detection to produce its weight and 90% interval; every aggregate in the app is a sum over these weights.

- API: FastAPI endpoints for region statistics, calendars, anomalies, trends, exposure and exports, with response caching, deployed serverless on Modal.

- Front end: Next.js 16 / React 19 / TypeScript with MapLibre GL for drawing and mapping (NASA GIBS Blue Marble and Black Marble, Sentinel-2 cloudless, OpenFreeMap and AWS terrain tiles) and ECharts for calendars, time series and distributions; deployed on Vercel.

USER WORKFLOW

1. Choose a preset region or draw any polygon on the globe.

2. FireLedger returns the harmonized monthly and daily record since November 2000, the current-month anomaly with its robust z-score, the season profile and the long-term trend.

3. Reliability badges, blind-spot and orbit-drift flags tell the user how far each number can be trusted.

4. Results can be exported as CSV (per hotspot, with weights and intervals) or as an image for reports and briefings.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Sensor physics: pixel size, scan-angle growth of the footprint, overpass times and day/night detection differences between MODIS and VIIRS.

- Sampling bias: revisit frequency, swath gaps and cloud cover, addressed through matched observation days.

- Sparse data: shrinkage so that cells with few fires borrow strength from their region instead of producing unstable factors.

- Non-vegetation heat: gas flares, volcanoes and industry separated so they do not distort wildfire statistics.

- Transparency: uncertainty, validation metrics and known limits are shown in the app, not only in documentation.

- Continuity: the method is anchored to NOAA-20, so the record continues as MODIS and S-NPP retire.

FUTURE WORK

Extending the chain to NOAA-21 VIIRS, adding fire radiative energy as a harmonized quantity, and offering automated alerts when an area's current month exceeds its historical range.
